Shape-Constrained Tensor Product Smooth of Two Covariates

Source: R/scte.R
scte.Rd

Constructs a smooth function of two covariates that has a shape in one of them for every value of the other, or a shape in each: monotone, convex or concave, or monotone and convex or concave together. The term enters the formula of any distribution parameter, like te().

Usage

scte(
  x,
  z,
  shapes = list(shape_increasing(), NULL),
  smooths = basis7::bspline_smooth(k = 6),
  by = NULL,
  by_hyper = c("shared", "level"),
  hyper = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  point = NULL,
  label = NULL
)

Arguments

x, z

The covariates, bare names or expressions in the data.

shapes

A list of two elements, for x and for z: each is a monotone shape (shape_increasing(), shape_decreasing()), a curvature shape (shape_convex(), shape_concave(), shape_increasing_convex() and the other three combinations) or NULL for a free margin, and at least one is a shape. A monotone shape may set min_slope, a single value, and then the derivative in its covariate is at least min_slope in absolute value everywhere. A shape may set value, the value of the surface along the line at that value of its covariate (see Details); it takes neither a slope at a point nor values by level.

smooths

A basis7 smoother whose basis is a B-spline, or a list of two, one per covariate: basis7::bspline_smooth() (the default, with six basis functions) or basis7::pspline_smooth(). Only the bases are used.

by

An optional factor or numeric variable, given as a bare name or an expression in the data, as in s().

by_hyper

With a factor by, whether the levels share the two smoothing parameters ("shared", the default) or each level has its own pair ("level").

hyper

NULL to estimate the smoothing parameters, or values at which to hold them, named lambda1 and lambda2 (with the level appended under by_hyper = "level", as lambda1.a).

id

NULL, or strings shared with other terms whose smoothing parameters are the same, named as hyper.

point

NULL, or the value of the surface at one point, as c(<x> = a, <z> = b, value = v) with the covariates as written in the call, or unnamed in that order.

label

The term's label; NULL builds scte(<x>, <z>) from the call.

Value

An unbuilt ScteTerm.

The construction

Each covariate is expanded in the B-spline basis of its smoother, and the surface is \(f(x, z) = B_x(x)^\top \Theta B_z(z)\) with \(\Theta\) the \(K_x \times K_z\) matrix of the tensor-product coefficients. A margin with a shape writes its direction of \(\Theta\) through the map \(A\) of that shape on the Greville abscissae of its basis, as scs() does for one covariate: the coordinates that the shape constrains (the increments of a monotone shape, the second differences of a convex or concave one) are nonnegative through the inverse of the log link, and the others (the level, and the slope of a plain curvature) are free. A minimum slope bounds the elements of \(B\) on a coordinate that is constrained in that direction and free in the other: the slope of a column of \(\Theta\) is a convex combination of them, and the elements constrained in both directions add to it.

With the shape on \(x\) alone, \(\Theta = A_x B\). Every column of \(\Theta\) has the shape, and since the basis in \(z\) is nonnegative and sums to one, \(f(\cdot, z)\) is a convex combination of the columns and has the shape for every \(z\). The rows of \(B\) on the free coordinates of the shape are free functions of \(z\); the coefficients of the level row sum to zero, the constant being left to the intercept of the model.

With shapes on both margins, \(\Theta = A_x B A_z^\top\). Every column of \(\Theta\) has the shape in \(x\) when an element \(b_{jk}\) on a coordinate \(j\) constrained in \(x\) has the sign of column \(k\) of \(A_z\), and every row has the shape in \(z\) when an element on a coordinate constrained in \(z\) has the sign of its column of \(A_x\); the free coordinates of a plain curvature are written as the two hat functions of the ends of its interval, which are nonnegative. The shapes hold for every coefficient vector. An element constrained in both directions must then have both signs; the covariates are reflected (which reverses a monotonicity and keeps a curvature) and the surface changes sign where this makes the two signs agree, which it does for every pair except a convex margin with a concave one. For that pair the elements constrained in both directions are zero, and the curvature in one covariate varies with the other only linearly. The elements free in both directions sum to zero, the constant being left to the intercept.

The interaction under two shapes

With shapes on both margins the cross elements \(b_{jk}\) are constrained as well, so the interaction has a fixed sign. Under two monotone shapes the mixed differences of \(\Theta\) are nonnegative when both margins are increasing or both decreasing, and nonpositive when one is increasing and the other decreasing. A surface that is increasing in both covariates with a negative interaction, such as \(x + z - xz/2\), is not of this form, and the fit is biased for it; with the shape on one margin the interaction is free. The construction of two monotone margins is that of Pya and Wood (2015).

A value along a line or at a point

The shape of a margin may carry a value, value = c(at = a, value = v) as in scs(), and then \(f(a, z) = v\) for every \(z\) (or \(f(x, a) = v\) for every \(x\) when the shape is on \(z\)). With \(r\) the row of the basis of \(x\) at \(a\) times the map of its shape, the condition is \(r B = c\) for the coordinates \(c\) of the constant \(v\) in the other margin. In each column of \(B\) that has a free element, one free element (the level where it enters) is written in terms of the others, and the condition is exact. In a column without a free element \(c\) is zero and every element with \(r_j \ne 0\) is zero, since all of them have the sign of the shapes. When the other margin is free every column has a free element, and the value removes the free function of \(z\) at \(x = a\). When the other margin has a shape, the elements on the coordinates of \(x\) that the basis at \(a\) touches are zero in the columns constrained in \(z\): the surface is flat in \(z\) over that band, and under two monotone shapes of the same direction over the whole side of \(a\) towards the start of the basis. At an end of the interval the band is the first coefficient alone.

The argument point fixes the value of the surface at one point, \(f(a, b) = v\): the contribution is \(v + (W(x, z) - W(a, b))\,b\), the number of coefficients is unchanged, and under a numeric by the level of \(f\) is no longer a coefficient. With an intercept in the model a value other than zero moves only the level that the intercept would carry. The term takes one value: a line or a point. A point or a line outside the interval of the basis is an error that names its bounds.

The penalty

Two smoothing parameters, lambda1 and lambda2, are selected with the rest of the model. lambda1 penalizes the first differences of the constrained coordinates of \(\gamma\) along \(x\), and lambda2 those along \(z\); the free row or column has the second differences of its coefficients along its own direction under the smoothing parameter of that direction.

Varying the surface by another variable

A factor by gives one surface per level, each with the shapes of shapes, and the level means come from the factor written in the formula; the coefficients are named <label>.<level>.g1, and so on. Under by_hyper = "level" each level has its own pair of smoothing parameters, named lambda1.<level> and lambda2.<level>. A numeric by \(w\) gives the varying-coefficient term \(w\,f(x, z)\): the level of \(f\) is then a free and unpenalized coefficient, <label>.const, and the default label is scte(x, z):w.

Prediction outside the data

Beyond the interval of a basis the surface is held at its value at the boundary, which preserves the shapes.

References

Pya, N. and Wood, S. N. (2015). Shape constrained additive models. Statistics and Computing, 25, 543–559.

See also

scs() for one covariate, te() for the unconstrained tensor product.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(150), z = runif(150))
tm <- term_build(scte(x, z, shapes = list(shape_increasing(), NULL)), dd)
f <- term_value(tm, coef = rnorm(length(term_coef_names(tm))),
                newdata = expand.grid(x = seq(0, 1, 0.1), z = 0.3))
all(diff(f) >= -1e-12)
#> [1] TRUE

# Increasing in both covariates.
scte(x, z, shapes = list(shape_increasing(), shape_increasing()))
#> <ScteTerm> 'scte(x, z)' (specification; call term_build() with data); increasing in x, increasing in z

# Convex in x, increasing and concave in z.
scte(x, z, shapes = list(shape_convex(), shape_increasing_concave()))
#> <ScteTerm> 'scte(x, z)' (specification; call term_build() with data); convex in x, increasing concave in z

# Increasing in x with f(0, z) = 0 for every z, and a value at a point.
scte(x, z, shapes = list(shape_increasing(value = c(at = 0, value = 0)), NULL),
     smooths = basis7::bspline_smooth(k = 6, lower = 0, upper = 1))
#> <ScteTerm> 'scte(x, z)' (specification; call term_build() with data); increasing in x, free in z
scte(x, z, shapes = list(shape_increasing(), shape_convex()),
     point = c(x = 0.5, z = 0.5, value = 1))
#> <ScteTerm> 'scte(x, z)' (specification; call term_build() with data); increasing in x, convex in z
